clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic GRHPR mutations reducing glyoxylate reductase/hydroxypyruvate reductase activity.
Unlike the liver-restricted enzyme of type 1, GRHPR is a widely expressed, mainly cytosolic enzyme, which has implications for transplantation strategy.
Biochemical hallmark is raised urinary oxalate together with raised L-glycerate (L-glyceric aciduria), the feature that separates it from types 1 and 3.
Course is generally milder than type 1, though recurrent calcium oxalate stones and progression to chronic kidney disease, and occasionally systemic oxalosis, still occur.
It is not pyridoxine responsive, since B6 responsiveness is a feature of type 1 rather than type 2.
Because the deficient enzyme is not confined to the liver, the rationale for liver transplantation is weaker than in type 1.
Management centres on high fluid intake and crystallisation inhibitors, with isolated kidney transplantation considered if renal failure supervenes.
reference.pathophysiology: Primary hyperoxaluria type 2 is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of glyoxylate reductase/hydroxypyruvate reductase (GRHPR), encoded by GRHPR. Unlike the liver-peroxisomal enzyme of type 1, GRHPR is a widely expressed, predominantly cytosolic enzyme that reduces glyoxylate to glycolate and hydroxypyruvate to D-glycerate. When it is deficient, glyoxylate accumulates and is oxidised by lactate dehydrogenase to oxalate, while hydroxypyruvate is instead reduced by lactate dehydrogenase to L-glycerate, producing the characteristic combined excretion of oxalate and L-glycerate. Oxalate overproduction promotes urinary calcium oxalate supersaturation with recurrent stones, nephrocalcinosis and, in a proportion of patients, progressive kidney disease. Because GRHPR is not restricted to the liver, systemic oxalosis tends to appear later and less frequently than in type 1, and the widespread tissue expression of the enzyme complicates the rationale for hepatic replacement.
additionalDifferentials: Enteric hyperoxaluria from malabsorption, short bowel or bariatric surgery
Idiopathic recurrent calcium oxalate stone disease
Other hereditary causes of nephrocalcinosis such as Dent disease or distal renal tubular acidosis
Cystinuria and other monogenic stone disorders
additionalInvestigations: Plasma oxalate measurement as renal function declines
Renal tract imaging for stones and nephrocalcinosis
Stone composition analysis confirming calcium oxalate
Assessment for systemic oxalosis when renal impairment is advanced
redFlags: Progressive decline in renal function despite conservative measures
Rising plasma oxalate suggesting evolving systemic oxalosis
Recurrent obstructing stones causing acute kidney injury
reference.prognosis: Type 2 generally carries a more favourable renal prognosis than type 1, but a significant minority still develop chronic kidney disease and occasionally systemic oxalosis. Sustained hyperhydration, crystallisation inhibitors and metabolic monitoring help preserve renal function.
pitfalls: Assuming type 2 is always benign and under-monitoring renal function
Offering a pyridoxine trial expecting the response seen in type 1
Proceeding to liver transplantation on the type 1 model without recognising that the enzyme is not liver-restricted
Missing the diagnosis by measuring only urinary oxalate and not L-glycerate
